Repeat kidney biopsy study: Immunofluorescence: paraffin sections of block B after double antigen retrieval (proteinase K treatment and heat-induced antigen retrieval); fluorescein isothiocyanate–labeled antibodies to IgA, IgG, IgM, κ, λ, C1q and C3c. 25 glomeruli are identified for this study. Kidney biopsy review 18.06.2026: areas of epithelial atrophy with uneven thickening of the tubular basement membrane (up to 15-20% of the biopsy volume). In the tubular space — protein masses, desquamated epithelium; in some tubules eosinophilic casts occupy the entire lumen; some tubules have a sharply reduced and/or absent lumen due to marked degenerative changes of the epithelium. In the stroma — edema, focal areas of interstitial and perivascular fibrosis (up to 15% of the biopsy volume), focal lympho-histio-plasmacytic cellular infiltrates of various sizes and locations. In vessels of various calibers — signs of spasm, dysmucoidosis; in some small-caliber vessels — signs of sclerosis/hyalinosis.
Vessels unchanged.

Degree of chronic changes (Sethi et al., 2017) — category 2 (mild chronic changes, total score 3 points): glomerulosclerosis 0, interstitial fibrosis 1, tubular atrophy 1, arteriolosclerosis 1.

Repeat kidney biopsy study: Glomeruli: 3 with segmental sclerosis at the glomerular tubular pole, adhesion to the capsule and/or proximal tubule neck epithelial cells, endocapillary foam cells in the adhesion zone of two of them, and hyalin. candidate_dispositions.rationale: The combination of nephrotic syndrome and three described segmental lesions near the glomerular tubular pole with adhesion, foam cells and hyalin first of all requires checking for a podocytopathy. Most other glomeruli are preserved. The glomerular immunofluorescence result is negative. Both findings are compatible with this hypothesis. The glomerular tip variant is an interpretation of the description, not a stated final diagnosis. The early description mentions proliferative changes and possible deposits. The later description does not agree with it. There is no electron microscopy report among the documents provided, and secondary causes have not been fully investigated.

candidate_dispositions.rationale: Nephrotic syndrome at disease onset and negative glomerular immunofluorescence are compatible with both minimal change disease and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis. At the same time, the description of three foci of segmental sclerosis gives no grounds to establish isolated minimal change disease. The branch remains for morphological review if the sclerosis/topography of the glomerular tip lesion is reassessed; it is not excluded merely on the reported lack of effect of pulses.

The morphological picture of focal segmental glomerulosclerosis does not by itself determine its cause. Adaptive, drug, infectious and genetic causes are kept as etiological alternatives within this branch. Age 34 and a prior course of unknown completeness do not prove a genetic disease. There are no data on a specific secondary factor or a family phenotype.

The first study describes periodic acid–Schiff–staining masses and basement membrane changes. The study conclusions suggest possible deposits that need checking. Monorestriction is not proven; the immunohistochemistry report text is partly damaged. In the later study, glomerular immunofluorescence is negative. Staining intensity of the tubular basement membranes was not assessed separately. The serum κ/λ free light chain ratio is 0.94 and within the reference interval. The examined bone marrow shows no evidence of myeloma. This reduces support for typical monoclonal immunoglobulin deposition disease but does not exclude other forms of monoclonal gammopathy of renal significance. Concentrations of both free light chains are elevated. The estimated glomerular filtration rate is unknown, so the cause of the elevation has not been established. Other forms of monoclonal gammopathy of renal significance, including proliferative glomerulonephritis with monoclonal immunoglobulin deposits, remain hypotheses that require confirmation in kidney tissue. Two negative Congo red results argue against amyloidosis; immunoglobulin light chain amyloidosis and myeloma are not confirmed.

Early mesangial/endocapillary changes, reactions to immunoglobulin A and complement component C3, and pharyngitis before the edema allow for immunoglobulin A involvement. IgA-dominant deposits are not established. In the later study, glomerular IgA and complement reactions are negative and the morphological description differs. Biopsy confirmation of IgA nephropathy is missing; primary IgA nephropathy must be distinguished from the infectious branch.

Pharyngitis before the edema, the early active morphological description and later leukocytosis make a targeted infection check appropriate. They do not prove a single infectious process. No pathogen, active infection focus or characteristic changes on electron microscopy are given. The later morphological description contradicts the early one. Possible IgA/C3 changes need to be compared with the clinical picture.

Two cellular crescents and fibrinoid changes in the early description need checking as a possible active process. The combination of these findings with a negative immunofluorescence result on another review gives no grounds to establish vasculitis. The course of kidney function, urine sediment results and systemic manifestations are unknown. Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis is not established. The dangerous branch is kept conditionally. If rapidly progressive kidney injury or pulmonary-renal syndrome is suspected, a separate urgent anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody test is needed. This is a mechanism separate from pauci-immune injury. A negative glomerular IgG reaction on paraffin sections does not by itself exclude it.

items.body: Concurrent conditions and parallel processes. “Concurrent renal tubular injury. Degree of functional impairment unknown”. A separate component/concurrent finding that does not on its own explain the entire nephrotic syndrome. Both descriptions contain degenerative tubular epithelial changes and protein casts. This is a separate component, possible with severe glomerular proteinuria or another factor. Acute kidney injury without functional data is not established. Hyaline/granular casts do not confirm myeloma cast nephropathy. “Leukocytosis with a left-shifted differential and mild anemia of undetermined cause”. A separate component/concurrent finding that does not on its own explain the entire nephrotic syndrome. The source reports leukocytosis to myelocytes and mild anemia without quantitative values. A reactive/infectious or drug explanation needs checking; the cause of anemia is not established. A negative bone marrow conclusion regarding myeloma is not a universal exclusion of all hematological processes.

items.body: Edema after symptom onset on 30.03.2026, daily proteinuria of 4.1 g on 23.04 and 5.6 g on 29.06, blood albumin of 20 g/L and total protein of 37 g/L form a nephrotic syndrome. The description of 08.07 contains three glomeruli with segmental sclerosis near the glomerular tubular pole, adhesion, foam cells and hyalin; the remaining glomeruli show no mesangial expansion or basement membrane thickening. Glomerular immunofluorescence is negative. This supports a podocyte mechanism and a possible glomerular tip lesion, but the pattern name is a current hypothesis, not the source's verbatim final diagnosis. Electron microscopy is unavailable, and the early description differs substantially. Causation and primary nature are not proven; reports of methylprednisolone pulses and cyclophosphamide do not establish course adequacy or steroid resistance.

items.body: An acute nephrotic onset, mostly preserved glomeruli and negative glomerular immunofluorescence are compatible with podocytopathy. At the same time, the three described segmental sclerotic lesions argue against automatically establishing pure minimal change disease. This alternative is kept in case the review clarifies the nature of the foci attributed to sclerosis or shows a different meaning of the changes near the glomerular tubular pole. Without an electron microscopy report and reconciled morphology it cannot be confirmed; the provided treatment information is insufficient for final exclusion on the basis of no response.

items.body: If the review confirms segmental sclerosis near the glomerular tubular pole, its cause still has to be clarified. Age 34 and the reported lack of response to a course of unknown completeness do not prove a genetic nature, but they require not equating the morphological features of focal segmental glomerulosclerosis with a primary immune disease. The package lacks family history, prior renal history, body weight, data on kidney number/size, HIV or suspicious drug exposures. A sudden marked nephrotic syndrome supports a primary podocytopathy more than a typical adaptive form but does not close these gaps. These are alternative etiologies of the same pattern; the genetic form is not declared reversible.

items.body: The early source conclusions only suggest monoclonal immunoglobulin deposition disease, including light chain deposition; they describe periodic acid–Schiff–staining masses, membrane thickening and tubular changes. This is a reason to check the deposit hypothesis, not a ready diagnosis. The early immunohistochemical description gives positive reactions to several reagents, a damaged label for the second light chain and intensities unsuitable for quantitative reading; monorestriction was not established from it. In the later study the glomerular reaction to each of the two light chain types, κ and λ, was scored 0, but there are no tabulated scores for tubular basement membranes. In blood, concentrations of both free light chains are elevated with κ/λ 0.94 within the given reference; the bone marrow gave no evidence of myeloma, with 0.2% plasma cells. This lowers support for an overt clone but is not a complete exclusion of a renal monoclonal process. In an undated conclusion the consultant assessed monoclonal gammopathy as unlikely. Two negative Congo red results argue against amyloidosis; immunoglobulin light chain amyloidosis or multiple myeloma was not established on its own.

items.body: Sore throat before the edema, early mesangial/endocapillary changes and two crescents, and the described IgA and C3 in glomeruli allow for IgA-associated glomerulopathy. IgA dominance is not established: this is an immunohistochemical description with technical/text problems, the repeat glomerular immunofluorescence for IgA and C3c is negative, and late light microscopy shows no mesangial proliferation. Hematuria, complement, kidney function and the exact interval between pharyngitis and edema are not given. Therefore IgA nephropathy is a conditional differential branch, not a conclusion from the sore throat itself.

items.body: A preceding sore throat, early endocapillary activity, reactions to immunoglobulin A and complement component C3 in a contradictory immunohistochemical description, and later leukocytosis with a shift give grounds for a reversible/treatable infectious alternative. These events do not prove a single infectious process, and the leukocytosis may have another explanation. The late immunonegative morphology and the absence of described deposits weaken this branch. The package contains no infectious pathogen, bacteremia, low complement or confirmed infectious focus. The check is important before further immunosuppression, but an infection diagnosis has not been made.

items.body: Two cellular crescents, fibrinoid changes and capsule ruptures in the early description need explanation. Late glomerular immunofluorescence is negative, but it cannot be mechanically combined with the early crescents to establish vasculitis: late light microscopy describes a different pattern, and early immunohistochemistry was reactive. There are no data on rapid decline of kidney function, active urinary sediment or systemic manifestations. The hypothesis has low current support and is kept because of the consequences of missing an active process. Two crescents alone do not equal clinical rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.

items.body: The early description contains marked degenerative changes and necrosis of groups of tubular cells, the later one hyaline-droplet and vacuolar changes and hyaline/granular casts. This supports a separate injury component that may accompany glomerular proteinuria, hemodynamic disturbances or drug action. Without functional data, acute kidney injury is not established. Protein casts alone do not prove myeloma cast nephropathy; elevated urine concentrations of both free light chains do not prove monoclonality. The reported 5% fibrosis/atrophy in one description and higher scores in the other cannot be read as clinical improvement between two new biopsies.

A response to infection/inflammation, a drug effect or hematopoietic recovery are possible explanations, but current steroid intake on 29.06 is unknown. The anemia may have a separate cause; creatinine and iron metabolism values are not given. A negative bone marrow study for myeloma does not establish the cause of these changes and is not a universal exclusion of myeloid disease. items.body: According to the KDIGO guideline, primary focal segmental glomerulosclerosis is characterized by the combination of segmental sclerosis of some glomeruli on light microscopy, diffuse podocyte foot process effacement on electron microscopy, nephrotic syndrome and no other established cause. Nephrotic syndrome in the definition includes protein >3.5 g/day and albumin <30 g/L. In nephrotic syndrome, thromboembolic risk assessment for prophylaxis must be weighed against the individual risk of serious bleeding; confirmed thromboembolism is a separate condition. Diffuse podocyte foot process effacement is not a specific feature of primary focal segmental glomerulosclerosis and does not by itself separate all genetic forms. Genetic testing in adults is selective, based on familial/syndromic features and clinical context. In infection-related glomerulonephritis, endocapillary proliferation, crescents and granular deposits of IgA, C3 or other components are possible. Clinical manifestations, a search for infection and electron microscopy help distinguish it from IgA nephropathy. Biopsy is useful when culture evidence is absent or the diagnosis is uncertain. KDIGO recommends prompt testing for anti-glomerular basement membrane disease in all patients with suspected rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. Pulmonary manifestations are not a prerequisite of this rule. Application to the case: The given daily values and albumin support nephrotic syndrome. The documents contain no electron microscopy report, and the search for secondary causes is not yet complete. This rule is insufficient to establish primary focal segmental glomerulosclerosis in the patient. Application to the case: Supports checking symptoms and individual risks; does not establish thrombosis and does not justify a prescription based on albumin 20 g/L alone. Application to the case: Supports history-taking and cautious etiological classification; the absence of documented adequate therapy does not allow calling the patient steroid-resistant. Does not contain a full list of drug/HIV causes. Application to the case: Supports a targeted infection check and review of deposits. Absence of bacteremia does not exclude infection-related glomerulonephritis. A pharyngitis episode alone is insufficient for this diagnosis. Application to the case: Only practice point 11.1.1 of the diagnostic text was read; the figure and treatment sections were not used. It justifies a separate urgent anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody test if a rapidly progressive renal picture is suspected, including without pulmonary manifestations. The patient's current kidney function and signs of pulmonary-renal syndrome are unknown; this item does not confirm her diagnosis, set test sensitivity or justify a treatment prescription.

items.body: In a retrospective series, glomerular tip lesions were often accompanied by nephrotic syndrome and clinically resembled minimal change disease or focal segmental glomerulosclerosis. Application to the case: A retrospective primary study; only the indexed abstract was read. It justifies reviewing the location of the lesion near the glomerular tubular pole and checking minimal change disease as an alternative. It does not contain sufficient formal criteria for glomerular tip lesions, a standardized steroid course duration or an individual prognosis.

items.body: The performance of immunofluorescence on paraffin sections after pronase treatment depends on the disease and antigen. The result may differ from immunofluorescence on frozen tissue. Application to the case: Supports checking methods and controls in case of discrepancy. The patient's sample used proteinase K with heat-induced antigen retrieval; the numerical sensitivity of the pronase study cannot be transferred to this protocol. The article abstract does not prove that this patient's immunofluorescence result was false-negative.

items.body: Assessing monoclonal gammopathy of renal significance compares light and electron microscopy, immunofluorescence or immunohistochemistry and clinical-laboratory data. In monoclonal immunoglobulin deposition disease, electron microscopy may reveal small deposits only in some areas of the tubular basement membranes. items.body: If no monoclonal immunoglobulin is detected in blood or urine, this does not exclude all forms of monoclonal gammopathy of renal significance. H1.rationale: The combination of nephrotic syndrome and three described segmental lesions near the glomerular tubular pole with adhesion, foam cells and hyalin first of all requires checking for a podocytopathy. Most other glomeruli are preserved. The glomerular immunofluorescence result is negative. Both findings are compatible with this hypothesis. The glomerular tip variant is an interpretation of the description, not a stated final diagnosis. The early description mentions proliferative changes and possible deposits. The later description does not agree with it. There is no electron microscopy report among the documents provided, and secondary causes have not been fully investigated.

H2.rationale: Nephrotic syndrome at disease onset and negative glomerular immunofluorescence are compatible with both minimal change disease and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis. At the same time, the description of three foci of segmental sclerosis gives no grounds to establish isolated minimal change disease. The branch remains for morphological review if the sclerosis/topography of the glomerular tip lesion is reassessed; it is not excluded merely on the reported lack of effect of pulses.

H3.rationale: The morphological picture of focal segmental glomerulosclerosis does not by itself determine its cause. Adaptive, drug, infectious and genetic causes are kept as etiological alternatives within this branch. Age 34 and a prior course of unknown completeness do not prove a genetic disease. There are no data on a specific secondary factor or a family phenotype.

H4.rationale: The first study describes periodic acid–Schiff–staining masses and basement membrane changes. The study conclusions suggest possible deposits that need checking. Monorestriction is not proven; the immunohistochemistry report text is partly damaged. In the later study, glomerular immunofluorescence is negative. Staining intensity of the tubular basement membranes was not assessed separately. The serum κ/λ free light chain ratio is 0.94 and within the reference interval. The examined bone marrow shows no evidence of myeloma. This reduces support for typical monoclonal immunoglobulin deposition disease but does not exclude other forms of monoclonal gammopathy of renal significance. Concentrations of both free light chains are elevated. The estimated glomerular filtration rate is unknown, so the cause of the elevation has not been established. Other forms of monoclonal gammopathy of renal significance, including proliferative glomerulonephritis with monoclonal immunoglobulin deposits, remain hypotheses that require confirmation in kidney tissue. Two negative Congo red results argue against amyloidosis; immunoglobulin light chain amyloidosis and myeloma are not confirmed.

H5.rationale: Early mesangial/endocapillary changes, reactions to immunoglobulin A and complement component C3, and pharyngitis before the edema allow for immunoglobulin A involvement. IgA-dominant deposits are not established. In the later study, glomerular IgA and complement reactions are negative and the morphological description differs. Biopsy confirmation of IgA nephropathy is missing; primary IgA nephropathy must be distinguished from the infectious branch.

H6.rationale: Pharyngitis before the edema, the early active morphological description and later leukocytosis make a targeted infection check appropriate. They do not prove a single infectious process. No pathogen, active infection focus or characteristic changes on electron microscopy are given. The later morphological description contradicts the early one. Possible IgA/C3 changes need to be compared with the clinical picture.

H7.rationale: Two cellular crescents and fibrinoid changes in the early description need checking as a possible active process. The combination of these findings with a negative immunofluorescence result on another review gives no grounds to establish vasculitis. The course of kidney function, urine sediment results and systemic manifestations are unknown. Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis is not established. The dangerous branch is kept conditionally.
